title: Reciprocal wiring gave no clear 20 Hz response prediction gain in 1,184 human cortical connections
abstract: We tested whether a reciprocal excitatory connection flag improves paired-pulse ratio predictions in an independent human cortical slice cohort. The sample had 1,184 directed connections from 23 donors at 20 Hz. Models held each donor out of training and controlled for cell types, geometry, amplitude, and signal-to-noise ratio. Adding the reverse call changed mean donor squared log-ratio error from 0.119407 to 0.119736, a relative gain of -0.276%. A 999-draw donor bootstrap that refitted the models gave a 95% gain interval of -0.001854 to 0.000472, or -1.291% to 0.397%. A fixed-prediction interval lay below zero, which shows sensitivity to the uncertainty method. No planned check gave clear positive added value. This extends smaller Allen tests to a separate cohort and protocol. It does not establish equal physiology or a causal effect. Slice selection, detection error, shared amplitude estimates, one cohort, and 23 donors limit inference. New code, aggregate evidence, a figure, independent checks, exact hashes, and external-data retrieval steps support reproduction. GPL source records and record-level derivatives are not bundled.

display.caption: Prediction errors, primary uncertainty with and without model refits, and planned checks in 1,184 human cortical connections at 20 Hz. Positive gain means lower error. Check intervals hold predictions fixed. The primary refit interval includes zero.
